speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: EXTERNAL AID
subsubtopic: FAMINE IN AFRICA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hardly need remind the House of the terrible famine that struck the African continent last year and continues to affect certain regions.

On that occasion, Canadians as a people really mobilized in coming to the assistance of those hit by this terrible blow. Their response took many forms. There was the remarkable job done by the news media, which made the public aware of the problem. The results of a survey released Friday indicate that 61 per cent of Canadians learned about the situation via television.

There was the work done by Canadian voluntary agencies, which tiredlessly expended time and effort under the umbrella organization called Africa Emergency Aid. Finally, there were donations from hundreds of thousands of Canadians of all ages, from all walks of life and all regions of Canada. As a Member and a Minister, I was particularly aware of the consensus in Parliament on the extraordinary measures the Government felt it must take and indeed did take. I am of course referring to the work done by the Canadian Emergency Co-ordinator African Famine, the Hon. David MacDonald. I want to pay tribute to his enthusiasm and energy and to his amazing talent for focussing the goodwill of so many people. I am also thinking of the contribution made by the Canadian International Development Agency.
Time and time again, when travelling in Africa, I listened to some very moving statements by Ministers, senior officials and even average citizens of Third World countries about the projects implemented by our development agency. I remember with considerable emotion that on the very day the BBC broadcast the first pictures of the famine, a ship sailed into the port of Assab in Ethiopia, carrying 36,000 tonnes of wheat sent through CIDA on behalf of Canada. I also think of the Members of this House who participated in a number of fact-

May 6, 1986
Statements by Ministers
finding missions to Africa and whose advice proved immensely useful.
Mr. Speaker, at a seminar we organized last year on the African crisis, we asked ourselves the question: What is going to happen once the TV cameras have left? That is the question I intend to answer today.
First of all, to remove any impression of condescending to the countries in question, I want to make it quite clear before the House that it is up to the Africans first of all to save and develop Africa. And since the last meeting of Heads of State of the OAU held last summer, we know they have the imagination and the determination to do so. The priority program for Africa's economic recovery which they designed is remarkable in its relevance. The African States have made it clear that their first priority will be agricultural development and continuing the struggle against drought and desertification. They have also confirmed their decision to implement policies for setting farm prices that will promote agricultural development and the well-being of their farmers.
Following this demonstration of firm purpose by our African partners, I wish to announce today in the House the launching of Africa 2000. The Government will thus designate all the measures it will take to meet the needs of the countries of the African continent over the next fifteen years and to provide them with the tools they require to achieve their recovery.
Africa 2000 is a 15-year commitment that the budgetary framework, put in place by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) last February, allows the Government to take in support of the development of the African continent.

The sum of $150 million has been released from CIDA's current budget and will be allocated solely to this operation during the next five years. This is in addition to the already impressive funding we have allocated to our aid and cooperation projects on the same continent. In the year 1986-87 alone, this will mean more than $900 million in transfers of money, goods and services by Canada for the benefit of Africa.
Africa 2000 will have three main themes: partnership between the Government and the Canadian private sector; the reorientation of our development policies; and finally, international consultation and co-operation.
By partnership I mean the Government's determination to work together with all individuals, groups and agencies in our society that are willing to become involved and do their share. This theme has been a favorite topic of mine over the last two years. I am convinced that to increase the effectiveness of our programs, we must have an association with the private sector. I am thinking here of voluntary agencies, municipalities, artists, schools, unions, twinning organizations and private businesses.

The voluntary agencies which took part in the Africa Emergency Aid Committee met recently in Ottawa on April 27 and April 28. They informed the Government that they wished to continue working together on projects of recovery and development in Africa, and they elected a committee to determine the ways in which their co-operative effort might function. In view of this, I wish to confirm that the Government will provide them with $75 million over the next five years to support their activities, within the $150 million allocation that I just announced.

This fund will be based on the Government's matching of public donations as suggested on several occasions by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly). I also agree wholeheartedly with their request for an early warning system, details of which I will be describing very shortly. Finally, I intend to give them responsibility for managing a program through which they can continue to increase the Canadian public's awareness of the situation in Africa. I am counting on the NGOs. I hope they will be our primary partner in operation Africa 2000.
In an operation of this size, I think there is also a place for commercial enterprises that know Africa because they work there. At the end of next week, my Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Hudon) will issue a formal invitation in Quebec City to Canadian businesses, asking them to become actively involved in operation Africa 2000. They will be our second partners.
Finally, a new administrative unit will be set up within CIDA's Special Programs Branch. Its mandate will be to communicate with and assist groups and individuals wishing to make a contribution by taking part in Africa 2000.
As to the media, I think they should continue to play their essential role by informing the Canadian public of what is happening in Africa.
As far as our policies are concerned, my objective is to ensure that by the end of 1987, we will contribute to the creation of over 2000 small projects directed at meeting the basic needs of African populations.
Canada enthusiastically accepts to make agriculture, reforestation and food security its top priorities among the development projects which it will carry out on that continent.
Such an approach must of necessity involve African women. They make up 80 per cent of the labour force employed in the agricultural sector on that continent. To that effect, I will announce next June a program I feel very strongly about aimed at bringing African women into the mainstream of development.
Also, I intend to set up an advisory group which, on the strength of the expertise of resource people from all areas of activities and all regions of Canada, will advise the Government generally on its policies towards Africa.
May 6, 1986

Finally, Africa 2000 will be an exercise in international consultation. Next May 27-31, will be held in New York City an extraordinary session of the United Nations to deal with the situation in Africa. This session will give us an opportunity to consult our African partners, the other supporting countries and the various multilateral aid agencies. Preparations for this conference are making good progress and active consultations are already taking place. To be both significant and useful, Canada's contribution must be part of a general action plan directed at the deep roots of the economic crisis in Africa. Out of respect for this indispensable consultation process, I will say no more for the time being.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members of this House will recognize in operation Africa 2000 the immediate implementation of several recommendations made to us by Hon. David MacDonald. But still more significant, I ask you to see in this first series of measures which I make public today and those which I shall announce in New York City our Government's response to the assistance request it has received from African countries who are determined to assume fully their responsibility for their own development.

speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank the Minister for providing us with a copy of her statement a few hours earlier than has been the recent or past practice in this House. Her Cabinet colleagues should follow her example, for at least this gave us an opportunity to read her statement and consult the many documents made available to us so as to prepare an appropriate response to her remarks.
There is no need to recall the terrible situation which has been faithfully depicted by the media.
In these circumstances perhaps it would be fitting to commend both Canadian and international media for focusing world-wide attention on the situation and urging the various nations to put pressure on their respective Governments. Regardless of the political regimes under which they live, I think most people were appalled at this plight and decided something had to be done.
Perhaps I might remind the House that, in his own way, former Canadian Minister of Agriculture Eugene Whelan had tried to warn Canadians about future events in Africa. As usual his remarks fell on deaf ears and not a single world organization gave second thoughts to the significance of the advice offered by our former colleague, Mr. Whelan.
As the Minister did on a number of occasions, we must pay homage to Canadians for reacting so generously to the tragic African drought.
Mr. Speaker, we must also praise our volunteer organizations from coast to coast. There are quite a few, of course, but I thought I would single out some of them as an example of what we Canadians can do whenever we want to work together.
Statements by Ministers
Among others, Adopt a Village; The King's College, Halifax; the Steel Worker Humanity Fund; the Caisse populaire du Quebec and the Caisse populaire Desjardins; the CBC. I also have in mind some regional TV stations, more particularly ETV Maritime; the Canadian Jewish Congress; the Save the Children Fund; Canadian Universities Service Overseas; the World Concern Canada Association; the Leger Foundation; Development and Peace.
I have given only a few examples, but I hope that the agencies which I did not mention will consider themselves included since the entire list is contained in the report of the Hon. David MacDonald entitled "No More Famine: Decade for Africa".
The Minister says that she is launching a new program called Africa 2000, and that she was asked not for a ten-year, but for a fifteen-year commitment. I wish to congratulate her because, as I have told her privately, it is a good thing to get politics out of the issues of foreign aid and mutual assistance.
The Minister tells us that she is giving us a specific commitment for the next five years. She is scheduled to appear before the Committee on External Affairs next Thursday. It is not a surprise. I can tell her in advance what kind of questions we would like to ask her. We accept that she has announced an allocation of $160 million in her budget to be spent within the next five years, and she believes, with justification, that the voluntary organizations will come forward with half this amount.
I remember what our colleagues who accepted the invitation of the Hon. David MacDonald told the caucus. I am thinking for instance about the trips to Ethiopia and other parts of Africa made by our colleagues for Humber-Port au Port- St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) and Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). These trips were made on two different occasions, and our colleagues gave to the caucus, on whose behalf I am speaking today, a complete report on the terrible tragedy which was still going on, and they also warned us that, when the time came to do what we are doing today, we should not close our eyes on this problem even though we can now feel international world opinion turn to other matters such as terrorism and radioactive fall-out in the Soviet Union.
I therefore want to take this opportunity, Madam Minister and Mr. Speaker, to point out that famine has not disappeared and that we must continue to show a lot of vigilance in these matters.
We know that the Minister has been asked to appoint a special coordinator. She is not replying today, but this is one of the questions that I shall ask her on Thursday. Will she consider following the recommendation which has been supported by all voluntary groups and which was analyzed by Mr. Michel Roy in a remarkable article published in the newspaper La Presse of Saturday, April 26, where we also find articles by Gilles Toupin and Jooneed Khan, and where Mr. Roy says that the Minister must expect some resistance because, while these proposals to help French and English

May 6, 1986
Statements by Ministers
speaking Africa are well received in Canada, there is also a lot of resistance at the higher echelons of the establishment at CIDA and External Affairs.
I have no final opinion to give the Minister as yet. Instead, I would like to wait for the meeting Thursday to see if this would not be the best way to continue the efforts that the Canadian public wants the Government to make to continue in this direction and to improve coordination.
Through my own experience, I can tell the Minister that she will meet a lot of resistance. There is also the Parliamentary Committee chaired by the Hon. Member who changed places yesterday, but who used to sit at the back of the House, the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard), which wants to make a complete study. That is in the Committee's plans for the future. What remains to do is to determine the budget. This represents a major problem since there are only some $2 million available and this would require a budget of $8 million, but I know that the Hon. Member for Guelph, who chairs the Parliamentary Committee on External Affairs and International Trade wants to make a one year study on all foreign aid programs, and I think that this is a good idea.
I would therefore like to tell the Minister not to reject out of hand any proposals which might be made at the conclusion of the study. However, I congratulate her for having responded immediately to the report of the Hon. David MacDonald. I think that it would be appropriate at this time to pay hommage to this man whose moral conscience is so well known to everyone in this House. Those who have come to know him, Mr. Speaker, know that he is a dedicated man, conscious of world problems. He is conscious of development problems, and those who had the wisdom to appoint him as coordinator will have cause to congratulate themselves today, because he has accomplished the extraordinary task of coordinating all those organizations, the public, the media and of course the various levels of Government, federal, provincial and municipal.
He took on a seemingly impossible job. He succeeded because of his talent, and I feel certain that all our voluntary organizations will want us to pay tribute to him today.
Much is expected, Madam Minister, Mr. Speaker, from your working session with the United Nations. You were referring to that conference that will be held at the end of May. There is no need for me to speak on that today. I know the Minister has very definite ideas and I encourage her to proceed in that direction. She has new ideas. I encourage her to even shake up the institutions and the Department she is representing, so that they will follow the direction she wants to impart. I know she is very sensitive to the issue of African women. Well, we will keep very close to the Minister and see how she manages. We will support her if needs be and blame anyone for not helping her with her projects. But I know that when she comes back from New York, we will have an opportunity to question her in committee. I am pointing this out ahead of time to the Chairman of the Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. I am not the External Affairs critic, nor the associate critic-I hate the
word critic-but I am my Party's critic for External Relations and CIDA.
I therefore hope that when the Minister comes back from New York, she will make herself available to the Standing Committee so that we may have an exchange with her. I also wish that the Minister will tell us Thursday, when she comes before the Committee, what she intends to do about all the other proposals. I noted briefly, late last night and this morning, that the Hon. David MacDonald has made 15 recommendations. The Minister has laid emphasis on about seven, eight or nine. I know she has her ideas concerning the others. This morning is not the right time, but I would like her to take notice that Thursday I will probably start questioning her by asking her whether she will be responding to the other recommendations made by the Hon. David MacDonald.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is also my view that when we look at the estimates or when we come back to the study on international development which my colleague for Guelph wants to undertake, we should summon the coordinator, even though his task has ended for the time being, and try to determine whether we should not have some new direction.
I for one support a new direction for CIDA, a new voice for that body, but this is not something that has to be done today. In due course we will do it; we intend to have a discussion with the Minister, and her officials, and reach decisions that hopefully will be acceptable to all Members in this House.
I would therefore like to conclude by thanking once again the Minister for responding within a reasonable time frame to the comments made by the Hon. David MacDonald in his report. I say to her: This is a step in the right direction. There are still many unsettled questions, but in my view we should not make this a partisan issue. It is a matter of approach. The Minister's approach may be different from ours. During discussions in committee, we will see where we agree and where we disagree. However, with the ultimate goal of helping our brothers and sisters in Africa, I feel we should not be partisan about this.
There is so much to be said. I know that my time has now expired, but there is a lot to say about the coordination that has to exist between Governments in Africa and contributing Governments, the encouragement that should be given to the Organization for African Unity so they will realize that together we can do miracles, but that divided there is very little we can do about those huge drought and hunger problems ... because this in fact is the great problem of the 20th and the 21st centuries, Mr. Speaker. Probably the great problem will not be nuclear power, but hunger in the world, and I know that we and the Minister want to address that now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), I wish to thank the Minister for her courtesy in
May 6, 1986

providing advance copies of her statement so that we were able to prepare reasonable responses. I would also like to thank her for her attempts over the last several months to involve Members of Parliament from all Parties in on-the-spot trips to see what is happening in Africa. As one who participated in a trip to Ethiopia at the end of the emergency aid program, I want to express my appreciation for that opportunity to see things first-hand.
I want to thank the Minister for her statement which indicates some very welcome steps to provide a continued Canadian response to the long-term problems of development in Africa. Over the last one and one-half years our aid program in Africa has been operating in a crisis situation. The immediate crisis has passed, but the long-term problems remain. We must now move into a long-term strategy.
In responding to the immediate crisis Canadians were greatly helped by the person whom the Government chose as the emergency co-ordinator. David MacDonald and his staff worked effectively with African Government officials as well as with Canadian NGOs to deliver Canadian assistance. Even more important, Mr. Speaker, through some very difficult situations David MacDonald was able to maintain the confidence of the Canadian people in the way in which our aid program was being administered. Canadians were prepared to give generously to African relief programs and they did give generously. However, they did not want to give foolishly in a manner which would simply prop up repressive military Governments or look after the needs of a local elite.
The situation in many African countries is very complex in such areas as economic development, relations with neighbouring countries, and relations with national minorities within their own boundaries. There are often liberation movements which are fighting against a central Government. The issue of human and political rights is very complex in many African countries. It is sometimes easy for us to stand in judgment in those situations. We would be very naive if we imagined for a moment that our aid could be kept Simon-pure in the face of all these problems.
While recognizing that there were problems and that we were not operating in a perfect world, we had confidence that David MacDonald was co-ordinating our aid effort in the best interests of the African people. We thank him for that and we thank the Government for appointing him. In spite of great logistical difficulties with transportation and distribution, we knew that our help was reaching the people who really needed it.
Questions remain about people who badly needed help but did not get it because of internal strife or because of inefficient local administration. These situations must still cause great concern to Canadians and people throughout the world who are concerned about the mass starvation which is taking place in some countries of Africa. These concerns do not invalidate the importance and value of our aid and the efficiency with which it reached people who needed it. We must now move from emergency aid to long-term development assistance. I
Statements by Ministers
think this calls for a more critical stance on the part of all concerned, including the Government through CIDA. I think it will call for a more critical stance on the part of all Members of Parliament as we look at the way in which our long-term aid is going to be administered.
I would like to recognize some of the positive elements in the Minister's statement. First, she recognized the right and responsibility of Africans and African states to establish their own priorities for recovery. This is not just a pro forma statement that the Minister made. It must be the absolute beginning for any intelligent participation by Canada in a development partnership with the continent of Africa. They have to establish their priorities. They have recognized that they have the primary responsibility. It is up to us to support them in those priorities and that responsibility.
Second, I want to congratulate the Minister for the recognition of the need for a long-term development program and for a financial commitment over the next five years. Third, I think it is very important to recognize that her statement talks about a continuing partnership between the Canadian Government and other sectors in designing and delivering development programs and in promoting public awareness of the situation in Africa.
The emergency aid program of the last 18 months showed that non-governmental organizations now have the capability to play a much more active role in administering development assistance. Non-governmental organizations can be particularly effective in monitoring assistance programs in sensitive areas where the local Governments have poor human rights records. NGOs have great potential for the establishment of locally based grass roots development. The 2,000 projects which the Minister spoke of taking place over the next several years will mean a lot of locally based grass roots developments which I think are particularly suited to the capabilities of NGOs.
As the Minister indicated, I support the program to match funds donated by individuals and organizations. This gives Canadians a chance to be directly involved in determining where their support should go. At the same time we should be aware that NGO-delivered assistance cannot be a complete substitute for bilateral assistance, Government to Government. It would then have the effect of undermining the credibility of national Governments. If development assistance should not be used to prop up national Governments, neither should it be used to undermine them. It is important that the use of NGOs be kept in some balance. They should not detract from the right of African states to determine their own development priorities and strategies.
The Minister referred to the general priorities of agriculture, reforestation, and food security. These have been identified by the African states themselves and I think this is something with which we all agree. We look forward to the Minister's announcement of a program designed to integrate

May 6, 1986
Tabling of Documents
women into development programs more than has been in the case in the past. Canada might have a better record than most other nations in this regard, but we have a long way to go before we have accorded women their proper place in development strategy and programs.
In a number of areas the Minister's statement fell short of the recommendations made by David MacDonald in his final report. For example, the statement did not mention Canada's action to ease the staggering $170 billion debt of African countries. Their debt service ratio is expected to be more than 27 per cent of their exports in 1985. Neither does the statement mention any Canadian policies for trade liberalization with African countries. She did indicate that intensive consultations are already under way with African states, other donor countries, and multilateral agencies on a comprehensive plan to come out of the special UN session on Africa at the end of this month. I hope Canada will be announcing at that session some real assistance regarding easement of debt and trade conditions. For Canada to be of real assistance to Africa at this session it has to take a leadership role on those two questions.
The Minister said nothing about MacDonald's recommendation that all African aid programs should be integrated and that there should be greater interdepartmental co-ordination, particularly regarding aid, trade, and finance. Perhaps this is not the occasion for such comprehensive policy announcements, but certainly these recommendations should be taken seriously by the Government and not simply filed on a shelf. I hope we will hear more from the Minister on what her intentions are regarding those recommendations.
Above all else, the Minister's statement has to be criticized for bringing such a modest contribution to a major world problem. David MacDonald said that if we want to prevent mass starvation from happening again, it will require a sense of purpose and a staying power far beyond anything demanded by the famine. On a yearly basis we will be contributing much less than we did in 1984-85. None of this will be new money; it will simply be taken from CIDA's regular budget. In September, 1984, speaking to the 39th Session of the UN General Assembly, right after he had been appointed as Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister said:
Our new Government intends to maintain Canada's commitment to reaching .7 per cent of the GNP by 1990 in official development assistance. Despite serious economic problems at home, we shall not turn our backs on the world's disadvantaged peoples.
Unfortunately, we have turned our back on the world's disadvantaged peoples because we will not reach that goal by 1990. We will reach it only some time in the 21st century. The needs of Africa, the needs of our world, are great. We should not be cutting back our development assistance program, given those needs. The Minister's announcement has to be seen in the framework of that unfortunate budgetary cut-back.
I want to close with a very brief image I have of Ethiopia when I visited there. We saw an orphanage with some 1,000 children gathered under three tents where they were receiving
a rudimentary education. Some of them reached out to us. To me that is a symbol of reaching out for help, reaching for life, reaching out to the developed world for our help to develop so that they can be in control of their lives when they grow up. Food would not be given to them as some kind of charity. They could be proud and complete human beings in a country and continent able to look after their own needs. As far as the Minister's statement leads us to take some first steps towards that goal, I commend her. I urge her to continue to work to develop a program which will reach the goal of .7 per cent of our GNP for development assistance much earlier than the next century.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, before the document is tabled I want to draw the first page to your attention. I have absolutely no objection to either of the appendices, Schedule A or Schedule B. However, I wonder whether it is appropriate for what appears on the face page of the document to appear in this form. Paragraph one says:
that in the absence from the National Capital Region of the Prime Minister or in the event of his being unable to perform the functions of his office
(a)	the Deputy Prime Minister, the Honourable Erik Nielsen, or
(b)	in the absence from the National Capital Region of the Deputy Prime Minister-or in the event of his being unable to perform the functions of the office of the Prime Minister, the next Minister named in order of priority in the list of Ministers set out in Schedule A-
In order to conform with the responsibilities of each cabinet Minister, I wonder whether it would not be more accurate to say in both documents that the designation concurring the Hon. Erik Nielsen for parliamentary purposes be the position that he holds, that of Minister of National Defence. What it should say is:
(a)	the Minister of National Defence, the Honourable Erik Nielsen, or
(b)	in the absence from the National Capital Region of the Minister of National Defence, the Honourable Erik Nielsen or in the event of his being unable to perform the functions of the office-
The reason I raise that is because the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) is a cabinet Minister by virtue of his being Minister of National Defence. There is no such function as Deputy Prime Minister within our parliamentary system. That is the reason, when the Cabinet was first struck in 1984,
May 6, 1986

that the Hon. Erik Nielsen was designated as the President of the Privy Council. He could then hold Cabinet rank and perform the function of Acting Prime Minister in the absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Since that is the case, I suggest that this document is flawed and therefore cannot be appended in its present form. It should be amended in order properly to establish the designation of the Ministers named in order of precedence for the purpose of acting in the absence of the Prime Minister. For example, Schedule A is absolutely correct because it sets out the persons who are to act for the Prime Minister in his absence or in the event of his being unable to perform the functions of his office. Schedule B sets out Ministers by Ministry, which Minister performs which function, and who will act in a given Minister's place. I therefore suggest that pages 1, 2 and 3 be altered to conform with the proper designations of the various Ministers and the functions they perform.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest for the second day in a row to the presentation by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain. I know that he was not present on the occasions when my colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence, was sworn into his portfolio. I was there. I heard him being sworn in by the representative of the Governor General. Whether the Hon. Member likes it or not, the Minister of National Defence is Deputy Prime Minister and was sworn into that particular responsibility in Cabinet.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-96, An Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the general principles involved in Established Programs Financing before I speak in favour of the Bill that is before us. It is a question that has disturbed me for some time.
As a federal Member and a Member of a provincial or territorial Legislature, I had the opportunity to attend interprovincial and federal-provincial meetings of Ministers responsible for health and social services. Over the years the federal Government has invaded several areas that, under the Constitution of Canada, are directly within provincial jurisdiction and reponsibility. These include health, education, and social services.
At some point in time the federal Government offered the provinces a deal that they could not refuse, by offering to pay half of the costs providing that the provinces rendered these services. No province could refuse that type of suggestion.
The federal Government has been unable to keep the funds flowing since these generous offers were made and very often it was the provinces that were left holding the bag when the funds dried up. This happened on several occasions under several Governments.
Very often it is the provinces that actually provide these services and pay for such things as social security, and the building and maintenance of hospitals. I have a certain amount of sympathy with the position in which the provinces find themselves and I understand why they are hesitant about getting into these deals in the first place.
In addition, the federal Government has moved in and taken up tax room in order to pay for its share of the funding. This means that there is not enough room left for a province to levy the taxes to get its share.
I was pleased when a Bill, similar to this, was introduced in 1977 by a Liberal Government of the day. That Government had to tighten its belt because it found itself in the same position as we are in today. One of the steps it took was to transfer tax points from the federal Government to the provincial Governments. At the same time as it was cutting down on certain transfer payments to the provinces, it gave the
provinces an ability to raise more money with this transfer of tax points. I thought that was a good idea.
Let me deal with Bill C-96. It is always difficult to stand up in the House of Commons or anywhere else and defend cuts in health services, although it is not really a cut but a reduction in the amount of expenditures that would have been incurred.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It is a cut. You were right the first time.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is the same with respect to education. However, we must face the facts. We are fully aware of the financial state of the Government of Canada, with the deficit we inherited from the previous Government. It is absolutely necessary that we get the finances of Canada under control. Therefore, we must take our responsibilities as a Government very seriously.
It is forced upon us to alter schemes such as the EPF. A structural imbalance had been built into the system and, if we were to continue under the existing formula, the deficit would become increasingly larger. Since we could not sustain that in the long run, the Government has had to take this initiative in order to regain control.
As I stressed before, transfer payments to the provinces for health services and education will continue to rise. There is no doubt about that. It is not a cut, as one of my colleagues from the New Democratic Party shouted out a little while ago. In fact these transfer payments will increase, and will continue to increase under the new formula.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Substantially.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Substantially so, although perhaps not as substantially as they would have under the old untenable system. We have to look at the federal Government's ability to pay vis-a-vis the ability to pay of the provincial Governments.
If one takes a look at the accounts of the federal or the provincial Governments, one will see that, because of the huge debt upon which we must pay interest as a federal Government, our ability to finance new expenditures is very much reduced as a result of what we have inherited. The huge deficit will continue for some time. We do not think we will really get it under control or stabilized until about 1992 under the projections of the Minister of Finance. But if we take the provinces as a group, we will find that their deficits are much less in proportion. They are running much closer to a balanced Budget. Therefore, their ability to take up some of the slack which might have been left is much greater than that of the federal Government at this time.
I want to argue in favour of the formula. I admit it is rather a complex formula in the Bill. It deals with two groups of GNP increases. I must say that I find it rather difficult to interpret. However, when we look at the results of the formula we see that under the circumstances it is as fair as it can possibly be. Probably more important, it is sustainable over
May 6, 1986

many, many years. We do not have to make further changes. We will not have to do as the Liberals did and bring in a new Bill every year to change the formula once again. It is sustainable. Both the federal and provincial Governments will be able to plan for years ahead knowing what these transfer payments are going to be. It certainly is my intention, and the intention of my colleagues, to vote in favour of this necessary legislation.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to comment briefly on what was said by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). I think he should have continued his speech in the same vein as he started, since at first he pointed out that he agreed with the formula negotiated in 1976 and adopted in the 1977-82 fiscal arrangements, because the formula included transfers of tax points for all provinces. He seemed to like that approach.
However, if we go all the way down the line, and I wish we did, the federal Government would no longer have to make any transfer payments because by that time the provinces would have enough tax points to be able to finance the activities under their jurisdiction.
I therefore fail to see how anyone can agree with the formula for transferring tax points and at the same time support Bill C-96, which is a cut back because it makes cuts in a formula that was established on the basis of both tax points and transfer payments. If we only had tax points, it would be impossible for the federal Government to cut tax points already transferred. So I don't really understand the logic of what he was saying.
1 would also like to point out that as far as new legislation to amend the formula is concerned, I suppose he was referring to Bills adopted by the Governments that preceded the Conservatives. All I can say is that Bill C-96 is changing the rules in the middle of the game. The fiscal arrangements on transfer payments were supposed to expire on March 31, 1987, and now this Bill changes the rules halfway through the game, which means that the provinces' budgeting for financing postsecondary education and health care programs has just been wiped out by a unilateral decision by the Government.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I am going to vote against adopting this Bill on second reading, and I would even go so far as to say that the House should refuse to consider this Bill in its present form.
In fact all these cutbacks under Bill C-96 will severely test the financial stability of most Canadian provinces. One may claim that payments will continue to increase, Mr. Speaker, but the formula had been established and the provinces have prepared their estimates on the basis of the gross National Product growth. But henceforth it will be geared to the GNP less 2 per cent, which means that between now and 1991-92 the accumulated losses of the provinces will reach $8 billion and they will have to learn to live with the deficit which will be passed on to them by the federal Government.
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Since 1976-77, Mr. Speaker, transfers to the provinces have been expressed as a percentage of the Gross National Product. On the basis of the GNP, these transfer payments have been stable. Ever since 1976 the transfer payments have remained stable and ranged from 5 to 5.75 per cent of the Gross National Product as a whole. Therefore the rising deficit as a ratio of the Gross National product cannot be traced back to these transfer payments, but rather to expenditures other than debt servicing which have gone up between 12 and 15 per cent in relation to the Gross National Product. In other words, if any adjustment has to be made it should not involve transfer payments to the provinces.
Second, why is the Government in such a hurry? In his November 1984 economic statement the Minister had indicated there would be no changes in transfer payments until the end of the financial agreements. Now he steers a new course, he is reneging on his commitment. Why re-open the 1982-87 agreements before their expiry date, in the middle of the game as hockey fans like to say? It amounts to betraying the provinces and leaving them to hold the deficit bag. Perhaps the Minister of Finance wants to say he has solved his deficit problem and pat himself on the back, but in fact he will quite simply have transferred his problem to the provinces. This is reminescent of Pontius Pilate's approach-to wash one's hands off the whole thing and let others worry about the problem.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, even the Nielsen Report refers to this issue in the study on health. I have here the English version of the Nielsen Report and I quote from page 13:

However, based on this review, the study team concludes that there are no compelling program reasons to reduce transfer payments. Thus, the announced intent of the federal Government to reduce the amount of transfer payments by $6 billion over the next five years is seen strictly as a necessary fiscal measure. The team fears, however, that this action by the federal government could substantially reduce its role in Canada's health care system. The percentage of federal government contributions to provincial health programs is currently at approximately 40 per cent. The team found no evidence that would indicate that our health system is significantly "overfunded" or "underfunded"-rather a balance overall appears to have been achieved at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, even the Nielsen Report indicated that there was no need for cuts, adding that there were no evidence that health programs were either overfinanced or underfinanced.
There was, therefore, according to the Nielsen Report, a certain balance. On this basis, the federal Government's decision to reduce its transfer payments to provinces will mean, in the final analysis, that the provinces will have to assume the deficit.
For some provinces, Bill C-96 will come on top of a previous legislation known as Bill C-39. Quebec will be more affected than other provinces due to the decision made last year concerning the equalization formula.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, when she introduced Bill C-39 the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) stated, and I quote: "The highest protection, the 95 per cent floor, is given

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
to those provinces which are not as strong fiscally as others and ensures that payments will decline by no more than 5 per cent from one year to the next. What the Government is doing in this Bill is giving Manitoba, Quebec and Nova Scotia the benefit of this 95 per cent floor for the purpose of making a lump sum payment which will assist them in the remaining two years of the current program."
That is what the Minister said in the House to reassure Hon. Members that Quebec would not receive less than 95 per cent of the equalization payments it had received the previous year.
The Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had said something similar on April 2, and I quote from page 3627 of the official record of the Debates:
I said that we would be equitable in applying a 95 per cent floor to the three provinces which would not be receiving the same amount of equalization in the current fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, we had received firm commitments from two Ministers; yet, failing again to keep its word, the Government has refused to give to the province of Quebec what the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) had promised here in the House, thereby forcing the Quebec Minister of Finance to raise taxes only to foot the bill which the Conservative Government has turned over to him.
In reply to a question directed to her in the House on Friday, May 2, the Minister of State (Finance) stated: "I think the statement made last night by the Minister of Finance for Quebec reflects some misunderstanding of the formula which was arrived at last year. All the provinces are treated equally and Quebec received half the equalization payments. But because the Quebec economy is doing so much better-"
Mr. Speaker, such a statement from a Minister of this Conservative Government is quite revealing of how poorly she understands the way in which the equalization formula should apply. And I just cannot understand how it is that no Conservative Member representing Quebec has exerted pressures on the Government to force it to fullfill its commitment and explain to the Minister what the equalization formula really means.
The equalization formula to share our country's wealth is a contractual agreement and it is even included in the preambule of our Constitution. I am not asking any special favours for a province, but I simply want the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) to keep the solemn commitment they both made before all the Members of this House when trying to convince them to accept Bill C-39.
Mr. Speaker, this decision of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance represents a betrayal for Quebec and I hope that the Conservative Members will use all their weight in caucus to call these two ministers to order and ensure that they keep their promise.
Mr. Speaker, this situation is so serious that, before resuming my seat, I would like to move the following motion:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"This House refuse to continue the consideration of this Bill, the purpose of which is to unilaterally reduce federal payments to the provinces for postsecondary education and health services which are essential."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few points about Bill C-96, points which I think relate to Government policy more than anything else. First, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) made a case for getting rid of the deficit by taking away or reducing two of the main economic factors in Canada, the need for a well educated and a healthy population. He suggested that by reducing the amount of money expended on health and education we could be rid of the deficit. That is kind of a negative approach.
There is no doubt that the policy of the Government as expressed in this particular Bill and in the Nielsen task force report is fairly specific. First, it is to eliminate any program that costs anything, or to pass that cost on to another Government. That is exactly what the Government is going to do. In this particular case the Government has decided to pass the costs of health care and of education either to the provincial Governments or to the students who are seeking education. If the Government does not do one of those two things, it will do a third thing. It will redefine the Government's responsibilities in order to bring the costs down to the absolute minimum.
If one were to study the parts of the Nielsen task force report which have already been put into policy, one would find that those three basic approaches are followed. The Government either eliminates a program, it passes the program on to someone else to pay for or it redefines the Government's responsibilities so that the program will not cost so much.
Second, the Government has proclaimed itself an open Government and has said that it is going to be consultative. In this particular case, perhaps the definition of consultation has been changed. The provincial Governments keep telling us that the actions taken by the federal Government in this particular case were unilateral. The federal Government proclaimed that it took this action only after consulting with the provincial Governments. The provincial Governments suggest that no agreement was reached and that they were told at the end of the federal-provincial conference that this action was going to be taken. They did not agree, and simply informing the
May 6, 1986

provinces does not seem to be the kind of consultation which was expected. There was no discussion, no recognition of the effects of this action, and no allowance for other actions which the provincial Governments might take rather than this action.
Third, the Government says that there will be no great disparities or inequities caused by this particular legislation. Nothing could be further from the truth. The Government knows that the impact of the cut in the rate of growth is that the amount of money that is available for health and postsecondary education will be reduced. The Government seems to refuse to recognize that the provinces will have to make up those costs which continue to increase.
The provincial Governments will have to find a source of income to replace the income which is being withheld by the federal Government. The provinces that have the money will probably not be affected greatly, but there are have-not provinces in Canada. There are provinces which do not have new sources of money and have a very difficult time remaining in a balanced position. In fact, in the last few years, some of the provinces have even gone into deficit positions. They will be affected and there will be inequalities in health care and education in those provinces.
We will be moving away from one of the great decisions that Canada has taken, and that is that everyone must have an equal opportunity. Every person who lives in Canada should have an equal opportunity to receive quality education. Sometimes we wondered about the Liberal Government's commitment to equality but the Conservative Government does not leave us to wonder at all. There is no doubt in anyone's mind that it has an elitist philosophy when it comes to education. It feels that not the most intelligent but the richest should be given the opportunity for quality education.
The Conservatives claim to believe that health care should be available and accessible to everyone. The key is whether they actually believe that it should be available to everyone. Obviously they do not believe it. Government Members are suggesting that it should be available to everyone who has the ability to pay. Also they say that no one should worry about health care not being available and that the access will be the same. However, access to quality health care is already deteriorating, and a reduction in the amount of money available each year will have the effect of further reducing quality health care in some provinces. Many areas will not receive the kinds of health service which they received in the past.
The Government has had a continuing tendency to forget that it made promises. In the 1984 election campaign, members of the Progressive Conservative Party stated that they were committed to sustaining the then current federal financial commitment according to the formula set out in the 1977 agreement. Also they stated that they believed that the financing of post-secondary education was an important priority for both levels of Government. That was a concise and
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
clear statement made by Conservative Party Members before the 1984 election, yet we see action on the part of the Government to back off from that promise, to forget that it was ever made, and to reduce the money which will be paid for postsecondary education. Government Members will say that they are only paying out less, but they promised to accept the 1977 formula which had a larger increase than the one they are allowing this year.
Health is one of those sacred trusts. It is amazing how the phrase "sacred trust" has become almost synonymous with broken promises. I will not spend a great deal of time on this matter because it has been well documented that the Government promised to allow a continuation of quality health care. However, it should be recognized that the promise of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of no reduction until 1987 was made after the election, to the provincial Governments and provincial Ministers at a federal-provincial conference. He promised to continue the funding. The suggestion of a reduction seemed innocuous at the time because it was so far into the future. Instead, he brought forward legislation which will mean that it will start to occur in 1986. The Government also suggested that it would do this in order to cut the deficit.
As I suggested earlier, we are being treated with an insight on how the Conservative Government thinks. It intends to cut the deficit on the backs of low-income and middle-income Canadians, on the backs of the "have-not" provinces, and at the expense of quality education and health care.
Let us look at what the Government has done to the tax structure. The taxes for high-income earners have been reduced, whereas the taxes for low-income earners have been increased. Now we see the same philosophy being applied to education. If education and health care require increases, no funds will be available for that purpose.
The Government needs to look at this piece of legislation again and bring it back in a form which would allow Canadians to continue to receive the kind of quality education and health care to which they are accustomed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) has been going across the country to speak with and listen to university students, professors, and administrators. He is profoundly concerned about post-secondary education. As the Leader of the Liberal Party, he has been alerting the country to the need for a national approach to post-secondary education. He is insisting that we need to find a way in which to get the provinces and the federal Government to co-operate and to ensure that the moneys transferred by the federal Government to the provinces indeed are spent on education, unlike what happened, for example, in the Province of British Columbia where a large amount of the funds was diverted to other purposes than post-secondary education.
My leader wants to ensure that federal incentives to the provinces are arranged for research and development and that the promised targets for research and development are reached. He also wants to ensure that attention is given to strengthening centres of excellence, that business and school co-operation is encouraged, and that we increase our effectiveness in spending. That is the program of the Leader of the Official Opposition. That is what the Government is not doing for us. It is not offering leadership. It is simply cutting back on its promises and even on its agreements, as the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) so eloquently and so excellently pointed out.
Bill C-96 is a bad Bill. Simply put, the Tories in Ottawa have decided unilaterally to reduce or cut the expected and promised transfer payments by the Ottawa Government to the provinces for health and for education. They did not ask the provinces; they told the provinces. They did this despite the protestations of the provinces. This is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker. Leadership is needed at a time like this. The crisis taking place in post-secondary education is a major one.
If we look at the reports and the observations of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, we find this:
Enrolment pressures have continued to mount in the past year. Even though the total 18-24 age group from which university enrolments are traditionally
drawn is declining, the proportion of this group undertaking university studies continues to grow.
Even though numbers are decreasing in the population, the number of young people in that age group seeking a university education is increasing. The statement goes on:
Across Canada, in 1985-86, full-time university enrolments increased by 1.5 per cent and part-time enrolments by 2.7 per cent. The percentage increase would no doubt have been higher if some universities had not been compelled to impose over-all limits on enrolments.
The list of difficulties facing universities grows. The unacceptably high faculty-student ratios, the outdated research equipment in some of our laboratories, the continuing concern relative to the brain drain of some of brightest and best researchers, the aging of our professoriate, the weakened library collections and the physical plants in disrepair have all been well documented. The universities do not seek sympathy or futher analysis. They seek and expect solutions.
Solutions require leadership. The problem unfortunately is that the Government is not giving leadership on how to deal with the question of post-secondary education and research. Rather it is simply dealing with budgets and unilaterally announcing a cut in the expected transfer payments that were supposed to have been made this year, thus breaking agreements with the provinces and cutting funds for future years. That is not leadership, Mr. Speaker. It is a betrayal of promises and it is a lack of responsibility at a time when a grave crisis faces the nation.
As this applies to general financing, it also applies and strikes universities in the area of research, which is such an important part of the life of universities. The Government not only through this Bill is assailing the foundation of the future of the universities and colleages but it is also, through other actions, complementing this, not providing the kind of leadership promised in the area of research.
Speaking on behalf of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the President of the Manitoba University, Arnold Naimark, noted that the latest move by the federal Government relating to guaranteed funding for the three granting councils responsible for most of the research in Canada will mean they will end up with less money in real terms than at present. This is an absolutely staggering result of the latest decision of the Conservative Government, this time in the realm of research. In the words of Mr. Naimark himself:

"We have examined the announcement of the Federal Government and it is obvious that the guaranteed support of the Federal Government to council activities will not be increased during the next five years. Even with an inflation rate of 4 per cent, in 1990-91, the purchasing power of the councils' budgets will in fact be 18 per cent lower than it is now."

With the decimation of our post-secondary universities on the one hand, and of the money they need for research on the other hand, which is not in this Bill, we have a double assault on our post-secondary educational system. This is devastating because we all know the future of Canada's economy depends
May 6, 1986

upon a very healthy and growing post-secondary educational system.
Mr. Don Savage, General Secretary of the Canadian Association of University Teachers, said that if we are to progress economically as a nation we will need more not fewer university graduates in science, engineering, and business management. If we are to survive in a competitive and frequently hostile world, we will have to know the cultures, history, politics and languages of our friends, our competitors, and our enemies. If we are to make any mark in the history of the world, all of this effort must be suffused with the ideals of our civilization, its history, its philosophy, and its literature. Our political leaders, said Mr. Savage, seem incapable of finding a way to fund the universities we need. That is an assessment which I am afraid is appearing to be all too true when we look at Bill C-96.
We certainly hope the Government will rethink its position on this, go back and fulfil the promises it made to the electorate on the matter of maintaining the level of at least the 1977 funding formula. We hope the Government will look at the promises to and agreement it made for this past year with the provinces, and at least fulfil them. It would be wise for the Government to do these things.
Everyone knows colleges and universities are in deep trouble right across the country. For that matter, since this Bill also deals with the medical situation as well as transfers to the provinces for the post-secondary educational fields, the Government should stop starving hospitals and medical centres. The Government must stop passing the buck to the provinces. It must give leadership and keep the promises it made in the last election.
I appeal to the Government and to the Members of Parliament who belong to the Government caucus, to drop Bill C-96 or vastly modify it and keep their pledge to the future of our country. Stop selling us out. Do not let us and our young people become slaves of other nations, hewers of wood and drawers of water, because we have failed to give to our young people the knowledge and the skills and the research to do the job. Give us the educational system we need.
If the Government will renegotiate and discuss with the provinces what can be done to work out co-operatively the future of post-secondary education, that will be a greater contribution by far than by merely passing Bills that cut back on the Government's own problems of the deficit here in Ottawa. Let us work out in dialogue with the provinces how we might co-operatively work together to guarantee a future for your young people. Let us not, together with the provinces, pass the buck on to the young people. Let us be brave and take on the responsibility of working together.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to make some comments regarding Bill C-96, a Bill which has to be identified as a Bill of betrayal to the young people of Canada, to the universities and colleges, vocational schools and educational institutes of
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Canada. It is a betrayal of the health care system and the people of Canada.
I recall a number of occasions when members of the Government opposite and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that the Government was going to commit itself to improving the health care and post-secondary educational systems of Canada. Bill C-96 cuts back on increases which should be going to our post-secondary education institutions and to health care across the country. Regardless of how you cut it, that is what this Bill is all about. Due to this Bill, in the next five years $6 billion which would normally have gone to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education will not be going to them.
In this fiscal year alone $318.9 million which should have been transferred to the provinces for post-secondary education will not be transferred. That is what the Department of Finance has told us and I thank it for laying out, in a very clear fashion, what the cut-backs will mean to the provinces. Next year that amount will escalate to $680 million. The following year over $1 billion will not be transferred to the provinces. Over the next five years about $6 billion will not be transferred to the provinces.
I do not know what kind of sign that gives the people of Canada. I do not know what kind of signal members of the Government are sending out to Canadians. The signal I receive is that the Government believes it is spending too much on colleges, universities, and institutes and is, therefore, going to cut back on its spending. The Government says that it cannot afford such expenditures. If the truth were to be known, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is a Member in the House of Commons who would not say that the most important natural resource in our country is our people, especially the young people who wish to be trained and educated to take their rightful role in our society in this and future decades. That, however, will not be the result of this particular Bill. Things will not improve.
I was in my constituency on the weekend. The headline in the local newspaper in Kamloops, British Columbia, read: "Major Cuts from College Funding". The article indicates that there will be a cut of $500,000 to Caribou College in Kamloops, British Columbia. Over the last four years that college has experienced a 16 per cent increase in enrolment. Yet it had its base budget cut by 11 per cent over that same period. It has more students but less money. The news this year is that a further $.5 million will be cut from its budget.
Materials used in education and health care lead the inflationary syndrome. Their cost tends to increase faster than the general rate of inflation. When the ravages of inflation are taken into consideration, the cuts to education and health care are even greater than the figures indicate.
There is something peculiar happening in the country as a result of this legislation. When this Bill was introduced by the

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) not long ago, it was done so with no real consultation about what impact it would have on the people in the provinces of Canada. It was unilaterally announced that the Government would be cutting back on post-secondary education. When the Prime Minister spoke of a new co-operative federalism, a new approach to doing business with the provinces, and a new openness of Government, we did not anticipate that it meant unilateral decisions which would have a very negative impact on the people of Canada, particularly in terms of the ability of provinces to provide health care and post-secondary education.
This is round two of this process. Not long ago when the Liberals were governing Canada they introduced cut-backs in post-secondary education as part of their six and five program. At the time we felt that that was an inappropriate move. My colleagues in the New Democratic Party, to the last individual, stood up and said that that was not the kind of action a country should be taking if it hoped to remain competitive and play its rightful role as a western industrialized nation. However, that is what the Liberals decided to do.
At that time the present Minister of Finance stood up in the House and spoke out against that. I do not have sufficient time to quote him, but he spoke vociferously against that action. The present chairman of the finance committee, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), almost had a heart attack. We thought he would not make it through his 20-minute speech because he was so worked up about what this would do to the young people of Canada. The present Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) stood up in his flashy and flamboyant way. Members for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) and Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) spoke against the legislation.
The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) from Newfoundland said:
Mr. Speaker, this is a deplorable piece of legislation because the principle of it is one of betrayal. The Bill betrays the provinces of Canada, the provincial Governments of Canada and betrays the universities of Canada. It betrays postsecondary institutions of Canada. It betrays the young people of Canada and illustrates rank hypocrisy in the actions of the Government.
He is now doing exactly the same thing. Then he went on about the hypocrisy and betrayal of it all. Now the tables are reversed except that the Government is not proposing a program to last for only two years; this is to be permanent. It will continue year after year. We say that it will cost us $6 billion over the next five years. We can extend that and say that it will cost us $8 billion over the next eight years, and so on.
The Government is saying that it does not plan to provide equal opportunities for the young people of Canada relative to other countries. Most western industrialized nations are investing heavily in post-secondary education and research and development. They are training their young people and retraining their workers. They are providing for education in
universities and colleges to lead to reseach and development for the production of a variety of products and commodities. Canada stands alone in saying that it will not be providing those increases like everyone else. Canada will not be participating in educating its people as are the other countries with which we compete.
I do not know why the House is not filled with Members of Parliament from British Columbia standing in their places saying that they will not accept this. The Province of British Columbia stands alone in that it fails to pass along the entire amount of money it receives from the federal Government for post-secondary education. A report issued last year indicates that post-secondary education in British Columbia is not financed on a shared basis by the provincial and federal Governments. It is funded by the federal Government exclusively. That provincial Government provides virtually none of its own money for post-secondary education. It is simply not correct to believe that the provincial Government will make up the difference now that the federal Government is cutting back on funding to British Columbia. The track record indicates very clearly that if the shortfall is made up it will be done so by the students through tuition fees.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this Bill must be stopped. It cannot be allowed to continue. I hope that Members opposite will look at this reasoned amendment and vote in support of it.

As we went over the submissions we received from across Canada during the past several months, there was one constant and consistent theme. That theme was that the fundamental strength of Canada as a world trader in the future will be based on the brainpower and knowledge of its citizens. Our future will depend upon our capacity to tL nk, innovate and develop new products.
It is therefore ironic that I am here debating a Bill which runs totally counter to that theme. It contradicts, refutes and negates that theme. It will have the effect of totally eroding the skils of Canadians. It will lower our ability to be creative and innovative. It reduces our potential to develop the brains, abilities and skills of Canadians in our universities and other institutions of higher learning. How can the Government operate on two tracks going in opposite directions? Members of the Government stand here day after day talking about their commitment to economic development. They say we must become one of the great international traders. At the same
May 6, 1986

time they are pulling the rug out from underneath the ability of Canadians to supply that trading competition.
I visited the universities in my riding over the past several weeks to talk to students, faculty and administrators about present conditions in our universities. Their maintenance budgets, which go towards keeping the halls clean and maintaining equipment at acceptable standards, have not been increased for four or five years. The research budgets, which go towards providing new equipment and books, the hiring of research assistants and many other things, have been cut back virtually to zero. As a country we have always believed that one of the major commitments we should make is that of broadening educational opportunities. Higher education should not be available just for the children of upper middle-class or upper-class families. The real strength of Canada has been that we have widened the availability of higher education to make it available to the working class of people, the poor and minority groups. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak once more on this legislation. I hope I will have other opportunities to speak on it, because the longer we keep discussing it, the longer we will prevent the new situation from setting in. It is important to delay this legislation because it really is destructive of Canadian policy.
Mr. Speaker, the impact of the legislation now before us is to reduce transfer payments from the federal Government to provincial Governments for post-secondary education and health services. A few Conservative Members have risen in this debate, expressing the view that this Government is not reducing health and post-secondary education payments to provinces.
But the fact is this Government has reduced expenditures. Let me take for instance Manitoba, where planned expenditures in those areas will be reduced by $235 million over the period to 1990. Mr. Speaker, that is a large amount of money, and that cut has significant implications for the Province of Manitoba.
In order to illustrate that reduction, I will now give more readily understandable examples. For a four person family in Manitoba, the reduction will amount to more than $1,000 over a full year. The reduction of federal expenditures on health services and education will reduce federal support by $1,000 a year for each Manitoba family. As another example, let me

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
say this reduction will be greater than the overall Manitoba expenditures on universities and community colleges. Mr. Speaker, that is a truly significant reduction.
Many Conservatives have told us how important it was to reduce the deficit, how important it was to have control over public expenditures, and nobody disagrees with that on this side of the House. But how should we go about reducing the deficit? When the Conservatives were fighting to get elected, they said they would reduce the deficit by cutting down on squandering. Mr. Speaker, that was a good approach. But why is the Government not following that approach now, that it is in power?
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of priorities. Why reduce education and health expenditures while increasing those on armaments, national defence? It is important that we have armed forces, but why increase defence expenditures when we reduce education and health support?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a look at this Government's approach and its implications in the area of health care. It is true that health costs are increasing considerably. But how can we solve the problem while serving ordinary people? That is the question.
And, of course, the Conservatives' approach is to cut down on expenditures now. The problem with that is we are going to miss the opportunity to invest in new ways of delivering health services which in the long run could reduce health costs.
Mr. Speaker, it is important in my view for ordinary people to remember that our health system is more efficient and less expensive than the American one. With the public Medicare system we have here in this country, the cost of health care takes a smaller part of the GNP than in the United States, and with better results. In this country, families do not risk losing all their savings when one of their members is ill. But in the United States, a family can be ruined because of one serious illness.
Mr. Speaker, the public health system in this country is more efficient than if it were run by the private sector, and it is endangered by these Government reductions. By cutting down federal assistance to health care we are running the risk of destroying the system in the long run. The approach we advocate would be to invest in health care so as to be able to provide still more effective programs and, with time, costs would go down.
Mr. Speaker, we have to come to grips with real problems in the health sector because costs are rising, which can only mean less money available for post-secondary education. This country needs a sound post-secondary education system because our economy is heavily dependent on well educated people . . . one more minute, Mr. Speaker!
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, all I am saying is that reducing education and health expenditures is a short-term approach, and we must look much farther into the future if we want to serve ordinary Canadians and lead our country to prosperity.
