Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words in connection with Bill C-96, which is an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977. I have listened very carefully this morning to the comments of the Opposition indicating, as they have done time and time again, that this legislation is aimed at reducing the contribution the federal Government is making to both post-secondary school education and to health care services in this country.
I think it is important for the people of this country, and the Opposition, for that matter, to put this in its proper perspective. We are well aware that this legislation, far from decreasing the total quantum amount of money that will flow to the provinces, will in fact increase the quantity of money that will be going to the provinces this year, next year and in the years to come. In fact, as a result of this legislation the transfer payments in relation to post-secondary school education and health care will continue to grow at a rate of about 5 per cent annually. If inflation continues to be in the vicinity of 4 per cent as it has for the last two years, that will mean that the transfer payments in connection with health and postsecondary education will increase at an even greater rate than inflation.
That is not to suggest for one minute that this legislation is only increasing the quantity. Hon. Members have quite rightly pointed out that the formula that was in place previously is being altered and modified and, as a result of that modification, there will be a downward adjustment in the total amount of money that would have flowed, might have flowed, could have flowed to the provincial Government.

If post-secondary educational establishments and the health care systems do not cut their cloth according to inflation, there will be a requirement to provide them with more money from somewhere. Obviously, it will not come from the federal Government, so it will have to come from somewhere else. They always have and always will have that jurisdiction as long as the Constitution remains as it is.

The provinces have guarded that right very carefully and very jealously over many years.
I can understand the concern of the provincial Governments that in the future they may not get as much money from the federal Government for these purposes as they had hoped. However, I am sure that when the provincial Governments search their souls they will understand what we are doing. In the last 10 to 20 years, provincial Governments have been using this same approach with boards of education, municipalities and all those to whom they pay transfer payments. In fact, as a former municipal politician, I am well aware that long before the federal Government started to consider the possibility of not giving the provincial Government quite as much as it expected in future years, the provincial Governments were cutting back on the amounts not only that they had promised to municipalities and school boards in the past but actually reducing the amount. I recall that in my municipality in 1970, some 80 per cent of the total cost of educating children was paid for out of provincial transfer payments. Now it is down to less than 40 per cent.
The provincial Governments know what is happening. They have been taking similar action for many years and they know what it is like to shift expenses and costs to a lower level of Government.
Of course, the concern is not with the provincial Governments but with the taxpayers themselves. The taxpayers of this country pay taxes to municipal Governments, school boards, provincial Governments and the federal Government. Everyone in this Chamber and throughout the country must pay taxes, and we know what it is like to have to shoulder that burden of paying for all those things that make up the vast number of taxes which we must pay.
The problem we are facing is that the expenditures that Governments have undertaken in this country are out of whack with the amount of revenue that is flowing in. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, although I am also disappointed to have to speak to such a sad topic.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the previous speaker going on about how difficult it was for the federal Government to make ends meet and hurry in trying to pass the buck to the provinces which, he said, perhaps they were not doing enough and perhaps should seek other sources of income, and he kept saying that the Government of Canada had to reduce its deficit. In other words, through this Bill and the speeches of Government Members, they would have us believe that by using payments for the provinces, the provinces are the ones who will suffer in the final instance, but what they forget is who will really be affected by the cutbacks we are discussing today.
This Government, after making a formal commitment that neither post-secondary education nor health care would be tempered with, this Government had the nerve to present this Bill and make cutbacks amounting to nearly $6 billion between now and 1990-91, and if we take 1986 to 1992, we are talking about more than $8 billion in these two sectors.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we Quebecers should be particularly concerned about finding out what effect this will have on our province. In fact, since the Quebec Minister of Finance brought down his budget and told us that the Government would have to forego $66 million in equalization payments for the year ending on March 31, and that it would lose another $82 million over the current year, in addition to this cutback

May 6, 1986
which represents $82.3 million in 1986-87 for Quebec, $174.9 million in 1987-88 for Quebec, and so forth-I think we can say that this amounts to an unilateral attack on a province and on all provinces, but if we look at ours in particular, we see two groups that have very few lines of defence. I am referring to two basically important groups, namely, the students who are our future, and the sick, who unfortunately cannot avoid being sick.
Mr. Speaker, these are major cutbacks because the Government looked only at the figures without thinking about the consequences of its action. What will these cutbacks mean for the universities? It will mean a proportionately reduced access for the poorer members of our society and an automatic increase in tuition fees, which will also have an impact on access. I trust that this was not done for philosophical reasons by this Government, but the result will be that the rich will have greater access to post-secondary education and that nothing will be done to reduce social disparities. Mr. Speaker, our universities have been strongly affected these last few years by a whole series of cutbacks.
The Government says that it has to cutback the fat of programs, but I can tell the Government Members that there is no fat to cut back in our universities. The didactic equipment of our universities is getting older and the faculties can no longer afford to replace it. In all scientific fields, such as engineering, our faculties have enormous difficulty in providing technological training at the same rate as technology progresses because their budget no longer allows them to purchase new equipment.
The same thing is happening in the hospitals. You would have to be insensitive to believe that the hospitals have too much money. If we look at the situation in Quebec, we find that many hospitals now have substantial deficits. It is certainly not by cutting back the transfers in these two areas that we can provide more equality and improve health services or education. These are certainly two areas where the Governments should make some improvements. It is obvious that the amounts allocated to health care are reduced once more, those affected will be the aged. It is obvious that pathological research will be affected. Yet, this Government had made a commitment to increase research and development and provide more money in the priority health care areas. What has happened to those nice promises?
As concerns post-secondary education, the Government did not consult the provinces or anyone else, but decided to make savage cutbacks while saying: It is essential to increase occupational training and to ensure that our young people will be better trained for tomorrow's jobs. Where will they get this training, Mr. Speaker? Will they have to go to private schools in the United States? This is one thing that worries me in this debate.
I can hear the Conservatives laugh. They have defective memories. They should remember all the speeches they made at the time of the 6 and 5 program. And yet, the 6 and 5 per cent program, the purpose of which was to reduce inflation,
was an unqualified success. Sitting on the other side of the House at the time, I could hear Members of the Conservative Party getting incensed and calling it treason. What are they doing now? What they called treason two years ago they call now financial responsibility. What a change in attitude! What a change in vocabulary!
I hope therefore that the debate on the amendment which my colleague the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has moved to Bill C-96 will provide an opportunity for the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall), among others, to recognize her mistake and realize frankly that the action taken by the Government and by herself has been premature, that their decision was unilateral and that it will have desastrous consequences on both the health care and secondary education areas which they had promised to improve.
One need only consider the proportion of the Gross National Product which the various Governments allocate to Canadian universities and colleges to realize that it went down from 1.35 per cent in 1977-78 to 1.24 per cent in 1984-85. This proportion will keep going down because of the Bill before us. In a changing society like ours where education becomes the stumbling block of the whole system, I feel that by deciding to sacrifice this sector, the Government is demonstrating its very short-sightedness. Mr. Speaker, the same applies to health care. We know that Canadians are demanding improved health care, but the Government again is showing its insensibility.

subtopic: IMPACT OF FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
IMPACT OF FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what impact will the freer trade negotiations with the United States have on the environment? So far the Government has not dealt with that question. Now that negotiations are under way, it is urgent that the potential environmental impacts of freer trade be assessed.
For instance, under a freer trade agreement there could be increased pressure from Canadian companies, and particularly from U.S. multinationals, to reduce the cost of environmental protection and resource management programs. In addition, wherever Government-industry agreements have been reached on subsidies or tax incentives for pollution abatement or resource enhancement, challenges could be likely under a freer trade agreement. This could seriously hinder federal and provincial initiatives on controlling point sources of pollution, hazardous waste management, reforestation, fisheries management, waste water treatment, air quality, et cetera.
It is still not too late to prepare an environmental impact assessment of freer trade, and I urge the Government to do so.

Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) raised a point of order concerning the propriety of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) answering questions in the event that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is present in the House at the same time. He made the point that while the Deputy Prime Minister becomes the Acting Prime Minister during the Prime Minister's absence, he cannot be considered the Acting Prime Minister when the Prime Minister himself is present in the House.
The Prime Minister answers for the Government as a whole and is entitled to answer any question he chooses to answer relating to any ministerial portfolio and any matter of policy. He is equally entitled to delegate this responsibility to the Deputy Prime Minister, a responsibility the latter would normally exercise as Acting Prime Minister during the absence of the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister may also delegate specific matters to the Deputy Prime Minister. As we know, the Deputy Prime Minister has the current responsibility of dealing with matters relating to conflict of interest and the guidelines by which Ministers are bound. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in the debate on the Bill dealing with federal contributions to the financing of post-secondary education and health care in Canada. It is particularly a privilege to take part in the debate because of the great importance of federal contributions in developing our health care and our postsecondary educational systems over the years. Those contributions were of enormous importance in the 1960s and 1970s, but very unfortunately they have declined in the last years. This has had the effect of creating uncertainty in post-secondary education and also in particular in our health care system.
I have only a few minutes this afternoon in which to take part in the debate by expressing my concerns.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Order, please. The noise in the Chamber is not fair to the Hon. Member; it is simply not fair to the Hon. Member who has the floor.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I have only a few minutes this afternoon to comment upon the proposals which the Government has put before us regarding contributions over the next years toward health care and post-secondary education. I want to take those minutes to comment particularly on the effect of declining rates of increase on our universities and colleges because it is there that the crisis in education, research, and the development of the country is most clearly to be appreciated. Our universities and colleges are important in achieving the kind of economy and society which we will require in the last years of the 20th century. Therefore, the proposals of the Government deserve very severe examination. We need to press the Government to reconsider its proposals and to open up the matter of financing for health care and post-secondary education as it deserves to be opened up.
Against this background of general observations, let us take a look in some detail at what has happened during the past 20 years in the development of support from the federal Government for post-secondary education. In fact, we could go back 20 years to a federal-provincial conference which was held in 1966. That conference arrived at understandings among the provinces and the federal Government for support by the federal Government toward post-secondary education. Under those arrangements the federal Government advanced 50 per cent of provincial contributions to post-secondary education to the provinces for those purposes. As a result universities expanded during the late 1960s and early 1970s. Particularly in the Province of Ontario universities finished their construction and were prepared to take in students. Enrolment in universities and colleges grew rapidly, and the support of the federal Government for these purposes was sufficient to meet the need. Through the mid-1970s the arrangements on shared cost financing of post-secondary education had been well developed under arrangements dating back to 1967.
All of these facts have been well surveyed by Mr. A1 Johnson who is now a professor at the University of Toronto. The current issue of Policy Options has taken a look at the situation in universities. Mr. Johnson considered what took place from 1966 -67 through to 1977. He commented upon the efficacy and upon the usefulness of the system. Then he went on to say the following:
This is what renders utterly incomprehensible, to me, the decision of the Trudeau Government, ten years later, to abandon the post-secondary education financing arrangements,
That one sentence expresses the astonishment of someone who has given close attention to the matter and conducted a study on post-secondary education for the last Government. He pointed out that the consequence of the established programs financing Bill, to which we are now considering some changes, had the effect of removing the shared cost arrangements between Ottawa and the provincial Governments. As a consequence, when Ottawa transferred funds to the provincial Governments, the provincial Governments were under no obligation to advance those moneys to the universities. They could use them, strings untied, for any purpose at all. As a result, provincial Governments have put less and less provincial
May 6, 1986

money into universities and colleges. They have allowed more and more of the burden to be borne by the federal Government through these contributions because there was no check on them or no obligation at all, although one would think there would have been an obligation of honour.
I should like to refer to the eventual result in the worst cases. British Columbia poses a startling and stark example of how it could be abused. B.C. universities received less from their provincial Government than the federal Government had advanced to the Province of British Columbia for postsecondary education. In fact, the Province of British Columbia was making money on established programs financing.
The result has been that Canadian universities and colleges have not received the funds they needed in order to carry on their programs. When the federal Government cut back on its contributions in the 6-and 5-period, it exacerbated the problems which had been created by the arrangements of 1977. When the funds universities needed were growing by only 2.5 per cent in real terms while the number of students enrolling in universities grew by 27 per cent and the students enrolling in colleges grew by 36 per cent, a new Government came into office and contemplated the situation. What we were looking for from a new Government was for it to say that, for whatever reason, the Trudeau Government made a fundamental mistake with the 1977 Act. We needed to throw out the 1977 Act and try to return to the arrangements of 1967 and ensure that federal contributions matched provincial contributions so that the university and college system of the country would again be financed on the basis it should.
In an era when free trade is the issue before us all, the quality of the Canadian workforce, the techniques in our factories, the levels of production and the sophistication of the production we want to achieve are important issues. From the economic perspective, the importance of universities and colleges to advance our basic research capability is paramount. I say that not because I want to ignore the other areas of social and cultural importance that universities and colleges also support-because as a professor in an arts faculty I would hardly be ignorant of those things-but to emphasize the enormous economic importance of a strong post-secondary education system.
What has the Government given us? Instead of fundamental reform, it has rejected the EPF arrangements and rejected the development of a system in which federal contributions would encourage growing provincial contributions and adequate support of post-secondary education. We see changes being made in the spirit of six and five. We see the federal Government reducing the rate at which contributions to postsecondary education were expected to grow. We see provincial Governments being told that there will be less money than they expected and that the universities and colleges will have to do what they will.
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
In this context we see another failure of policy. Mr. Johnson says in his article that it was not that there was any plan here for a different way of doing things and it was not that Governments were saying: "Let's shift the burden to students." That is an action, though, which the Government conceivably might want to take. It might want to think that families and young people should be able to come up with the resources to support their own education, but it is not something my colleagues and I would favour at all. We would want to go in the opposite direction. We would want to see assistance to students expanded and the amount of tuition and other costs students have to bear for their education reduced. It is not that there is any such plan made explicit. There is nothing here except one instance of a Government's desperate desire to reduce its expenditures. It is one more desire to hold the lid on things without any serious recognition of what the consequences are going to be for the country.
I see that my time is almost up, but I want to express most serious alarm about the consequences for Canadian universities of the established programs financing and call upon the Government to abandon these arrangements, take up the report of Mr. A1 Johnson and arrive at the kinds of arrangements that will give us the capacity in teaching and research which the country needs so desperately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak today in the debate on Bill C-96 to amend the 1977 legislation on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and, more specifically, the contributions granted by the federal Government to the provinces for secondary education and health care.
My hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), has proposed an amendment to the Bill, urging the House to refuse further consideration of a Bill whose principle consists in unilaterally reducing federal payments to the provinces for post-secondary education and essential health services. I want to say that I give my unqualified support to this amendment by my hon. colleague from Laval-des-Rapides, because I think it is absolutely intolerable that the Government, after promising it would treat the provinces with civility, would never act unilaterally, and would ensure that any decision by the federal Government would be taken after prior consultation with the provinces ... Well it is obvious that Bill C-96, the Bill before the House today, is a complete reversal of what the Conservative Government promised. Once again, this Government has failed to keep its word. Once again, the Conservative Government has failed to meet its commitment to the provinces of Canada. I fail to understand why there are no Ministers or Members from Quebec to protest this absolutely unconscionable decision on the part of the Canadian Government.	.
Indeed, according to the figures which we were provided with, the province of Quebec will lose some $2 billion over the next few years because of that decision reached by the Tory Government. Gilles Lesage, Legislative Assembly Reporter for

Le Devoir, wrote the following on May 3rd, after the Budget brought down by the Quebec Finance Minister, and I quote:
The kind and gentle Gerad D.-

-whom nobody would ever suspect of dark secessionist designs, is urging his federal counterpart to respect his commitments on equalization payments and to negotiate in good faith on fiscal arrangements, instead of transferring part of his deficit to the provinces, without the latter having their say.

speechtext:
Mr. Lesage goes on to say, and I quote:
He is calling for fairness, justice, respect for the Constitution and regard for one's own word. Nothing less.
Mr. Speaker, such comments by the Quebec Finance Minister concerning this Conservative Government are clearly very serious. And nobody can claim that this is another of those famous federal-provincial bickerings that implied hostility between a Liberal federal Government committed to serving Canadian interests and a separatist Quebec Government committed to serving the interests of Quebec independence. One could understand at the time that there were not only opposing views but basically conflicting goals that necessarily led to confrontation between the provincial and federal levels, to public quarrels between those two Governments because there was no way they could agree on anything.
But now, Mr. Speaker, the situation is altogether different. We have here in Ottawa a Conservative Government which of course is respectful of provincial jurisdictions and which is committed to doing nothing without negotiating with the provinces, and in Quebec on the other hand we have a Liberal Government which is respectful of Canadian unity and which is only asking that this Government live up to its commitments. Indeed, columnist Gilles Lesage writes, and I quote:
So, Quebec is in favour of a Federal withdrawal from certain areas.
The Quebec Government fully understands that, under certain circumstances, the Government of Canada may wish to withdraw from certain areas. I quote:
But it cannot accept such a withdrawal without negotiations with the provinces and, more importantly, without a compensation in terms of Fiscal transfers. It (the Quebec Government) wishes therefore a global negotiation of the major programs involved.
If Ottawa can no longer assume its responsibilities regarding some transfer programs, it should withdraw from these areas in return for a compensation in terms of additional tax points. The negotiations would determine the extent of the fiscal Field to be allocated to the provinces which desire to assume fully their constitutional responsibilities.
Finally, the Quebec Government considers that a formal agreement between the two levels of Government would be the only way to confer on the Fiscal arrangements a more permanent, stable, and less arbitrary character than the current arrangements.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from reading this article that the present Conservative Government is not willing to proceed clearly, objectively, even honestly in its negotiations with the provinces.
During discussions with the provinces, the previous Federal Government had considered the possibility of transferring tax
points. As we know, this has been done in the past. Tax points have been transferred to the provinces in order for them to better assume their responsibilities.
I suggest the present Conservative Government has assumed an unspeakable attitude, and that my colleague the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) had every reason to move a motion calling on the House not to accept this Bill at this time. Why? Because this Bill will affect all provinces and cause them to lose billions of dollars over the next few years because of a unilateral decision of this Conservative Government.
Second, because the Government is merely transferring its own deficit to the provinces, which is entirely unacceptable in the present situation.
Third, because the Government has acted unilaterally, without the consent of the provinces and above all has failed to respect the tradition of federal-provincial arrangements. And also because during the last election campaign, the Conservatives promised to observe current arrangements for transfer payments to the provinces, especially for post-secondary education and health care services, because as we all know, there are some areas where costs have increased considerably and the provinces have to foot a much larger bill.
Today, it is utterly irresponsible on the part of the Canadian Government to withdraw from its commitments. It is leaving it up to the provinces to cope with an aging population which means more expenditures and health care, and it is letting the provinces foot the whole bill for post-secondary education, a sector that is extremely important to a country that wants to hold its own internationally and that must have a well-educated and above all specialized population in order to meet international competition today.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that if this Bill is approved by the Government, it will be a disgrace for all those Conservative backbenchers who are shirking their duty, who are not defending the interests of their voters, and especially for that bunch of Conservative yes-men from Quebec who go along with anything the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) wants to do, in this case, deprive the province of Quebec, over the next few years, of $2 billion Quebec would need to adequately fund education and especially health care programs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the effect of Bill C-96 is to reduce transfer payments to the provinces for the funding of health and post-secondary education. This legislation should, of course, be condemned. I hear one of the Government Members saying that it is all going to increase. That is an argument the Liberals could have made. They, of course, exhibit their own inconsistencies of argument.
It is not really enough to condemn this legislation. We should be censoring the Government, not only for policies
May 6, 1986

inconsistent with the role and necessity of post-secondary education in the country, but for a variety of policies and policy failures which seem to be designed to place the university and college system at a level equal to that of a fourth or fifth-rate nation.
There are those who would want to address the issue of the funding of health care and the effects this legislation will have on the hospitals, patients, and healthcare workers of the country. However, I think it is time to focus on the terrible inconsistency between what the Government says it stands for and what this legislation reflects. I have heard many speakers refer to the fact that the Government claims to be committed to having Canada enter into the late 20th century competition in science and technology, compete effectively in international markets, and use secondary manufacturing and research and development to ensure that our resources benefit us commensurate with their value, which can be enhanced by the entry into the equation of human creativity and so on. This morning we heard of the concern of the Science Council about the failure to anticipate what the result will be of the failure to develop a sound science and research policy for the free trade negotiations and what could be the free trade fact of the future.
Perhaps it is time to reflect on what the universities and colleges of our country mean to us. There is no doubt that universities provide a place where basic research occurs and knowledge is expanded in a fashion which will materially affect our future economic growth, although we sometimes infer from the positions which the Government takes that it is not completely cognizant of the relationship between basic science and industrial development and the fact that one cannot contrive basic research in order to accord with whatever notion one has of economic development and the growth of technological industries. Although the role is significant, it is significant in a way which politicians sometimes cannot quite understand.
1 think it is time to emphasize the fact that it is not only technological and hard science research which occurs in universities. The university is a place where knowledge is expanded and new knowledge is discovered. This new knowledge contributes to the civilization, humanization, and economic development of our country. As well, we must emphasize that the university is a place where young people learn and teaching occurs. Leadership develops there, as do the people who are going to continue to contribute to Canada as a civilized place to live. It is also a place where opportunity can be gained by so many of our people who were not born with a silver spoon in their mouths. It is a place where people can break through the fences which have stopped them from making their mark in our society, a mark which in the past was determined by family background, class or whatever. It is in a sense a place of equalization of opportunity for so many people. Yet we have had a series of Governments which have failed to acknowledge the important role which post-secondary education should play in the development of policy.
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
A number of events have been affecting the university system. There have been a number of reports, including a royal commission in Nova Scotia, a commission in Ontario, as well as the A1 Johnson Report and the Macdonald Report. There has been a great deal of formal focusing on concerns in the universities. There has been some expression on the part of the university community about the failure of the federal and provincial Governments to arrive at an agreement for a system of funding universities and colleges in a way that addresses the very severe circumstances in which they are struggling. These circumstances have been a repeated topic of debate, so Government Members should be perfectly aware of the crisis in the university system.
The crisis takes a number of forms of expression. The most important is the increasing number of recommendations appearing in all these reports concerning substitutions for funding not being provided by the federal and provincial Governments. A recurring theme among many of these reports is the statement that universities can no longer continue to place the emphasis on accessibility which characterized the previous two decades. The argument seems to be that this has been done at the expense of the very best in our society, meaning those who in the past have had easy access to university by virtue of wealth or family position. We have reports which say that fewer young people should go to university. We have reports which say quite explicitly that the trend towards equalization of opportunity, which has characterized the last two decades, should be turned around. Perhaps we should have fewer of the poor, fewer mothers, fewer disabled and fewer minority members attending university because that compromises the ability of universities to do research.
There has been another suggestion, that if we need to fund university research, then let's hook up the universities to industry. Let's make grants conditional upon an equivalent contribution by industry. The universities should be more pragmatic, connected more to the economic process in the surrounding communities. However, what we will then find is that basic research, which is so essential to universities, is going to be sacrificed. More important, the university and college system will be steered in the direction of priorities established by business people and corporations which would like the universities and colleges to be their handmaidens. The results are clear. It would mean less emphasis on teaching. If the university fails to teach, then it fails to fulfil its mission.
I could go on citing the effects of no policy or bad policy or inconsistent policy, and my colleagues would have me continue as well. However, I see you crossing your hands, Mr. Speaker, and as a consequence I shall concede the floor to the next speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise to speak once again on this Bill. In particular, it gives me the opportunity to ask the

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Government to correct an error in judgment. The Ministers concerned should go back to their provincial counterparts, the Ministers of Education and Ministers of Health and Welfare, and get the proper input so that we can avoid the drastic effects which are possible as a result of this Bill.
Like every other elected Member of this House, whether Minister, Parliamentary Secretary, back-bencher or, as my hon. friend from committee would say, private Member, I have a fundamental duty and responsibility to respond to the needs of my constituents. With that in mind, it is kind of sad that I have had to defend the needs of my constituents on so many occasions over the last few weeks. I have had to stand up and ask for an employment equity Bill which will allow the targeted groups, such as visible minorities, women and the handicapped, real access to real jobs. I have had to stand up and talk about the competition Bill and the real fear of people in my riding, indeed across the country, about the concentration of power and the fact that there is a sense of powerlessness in addressing those concerns. And here I am again, speaking, as I did the other day, on a Bill which addresses itself to equalization payments.
I do not believe there is anyone in this House who does not have a real sense of compassion and concern for the health of our society and its communities. We are concerned about education, particularly the education of young people. I, for one, am also concerned about the education of women, particularly those who are coming back into the workforce. This Bill can have very negative effects on the lives and future potential of many of those people. When you cut funding for education and health care, you are damaging the quality of life in this country, a quality of life of which Canadians have been very proud.
As Members of Parliament, our pathway to this House has been people. Our success here is determined by how we are able to meet the needs and concerns of the people in our society. I think it would be very wise for the Government to reconsider its plans, readdress its programs, and focus its agenda by discussing these issues with its provincial counterparts. I can say in retrospect from my seat here in the Parliament of Canada, along with all of my colleagues, that it is my responsibility to react to and to formulate the laws of this land.
I see and I appreciate even more the partnership role one finds within the volunteer sector and this parliamentary wing of our society.
Those of us who ignore the groups which come to speak to us, the volunteers who give freely of their time, effort, energy, concern and consideration, do so at our peril. The volunteer sector fulfils a very vital and key need in our institutions, particularly in our health care institutions. They cannot do the whole job. The volunteers bring caring, sharing, thoughtful consideration, concern and interest with respect to the programs that we have put into place. They are less rigid, less formal and can respond to the needs of the citizens. Because of
the bureaucratic nature of our institutions, schools and hospitals, we must keep in mind what is being said to us. We are very vulnerable in the kinds of cuts we may make. If you allow this Bill to go back for consultation the institutions in the provinces are in a better position to start to consider where they may tighten their belts without adversely impacting on either the education or the health structures in the provinces.
We cannot just tell the Canadians to pay their taxes, we must decrease the deficit. You also have to consider the quality of life and where you are going to make up for what you consider to be the key factor in all your deliberations and all the policy positions, that is, the reduction of the deficit. The deficit should be reduced, and I hope that you and I together can find effective and efficient ways to reduce it, but not on the backs on our youth, their potential for education and their future, and not on the backs of the sick and the elderly. Hospitals are already overcrowded, and there is a need for excellence in these services and for the development of new and ongoing programs to meet increasing needs.
This is a society that is undergoing stress. There is tremendous need for mental care. There is tremendous need for facing up to what happens when people lose jobs and lose their sense of self-worth. We will pay more in terms of cost of service to ourselves if we are not wise, careful and capable in the decision as to where we will cut.
As reported at page 12888 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) what she felt and how she responded to the concerns that were expressed in the Quebec Budget. Her answer was the following:
-the Minister of Finance for Quebec reflects some misunderstanding of the formula which was arrived at last year.
I think this indicates a lack of consideration and concern, and indicates even more strongly the need to go back and consult with the provinces.
There was an article in The Gazette referring to a questin of mine, and although it does not attribute the question to me, I did ask it. "Quebec surtax not Ottawa's fault: McDougall". The article, covered by CP, says:
Quebec has misunderstood the formula for calculating federal aid for the provinces if it believes Ottawa is to blame for a multi-million-dollar provincial surtax imposed Thursday, junior Finance Minister Barbara McDougall says. McDougall told the Commons that Quebec received fully half of a special equalization payment granted to several of the poorest provinces last year, but because the Quebec economy is doing better than forecast 'the payment does not work out quite the way it did' at first glance. McDougall did not elaborate on how the misunderstanding might have occurred but reiterated that while the growth of the payment has been slowed they will continue to grow faster than the rate of inflation.
Quebec Finance Minister Gerard D. Levesque announced a $152 million surtax on companies, municipalities and provincial Crown Corporations in the budget he presented Thursday.
He said the surtax was designed to make up for a $148 million shortfall in payments to Quebec from Ottawa intended for health care and post-secondary education and as part of Quebec's equalization payments.
The article goes on to point out that Robert Bourassa said the following:
May 6, 1986

-Ottawa is discriminating against the province by denying it $66 million it is owed in health and higher-education payments.
Liberal MPs have also demanded in recent weeks that federal Finance Minister Michael Wilson honour a commitment that equalization payments to Quebec not drop by more than 5 per cent a year.
1 suggest that this article should be read carefully. The payments to Quebec should return to the 95 per cent floor. If this Government thinks they should be 92.8 per cent, then I would point out strongly that this is one more demonstration of lack of understanding, lack of good faith, and, as might well be the case, lack of goodwill.
1 heartily approve the move by my colleague to delay this Bill until it goes back for rediscussion of its implication for the provinces.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday when I spoke on the amendment to this Bill I mentioned that this was not a time to be reducing the total amount of expenditures for health care and post-secondary education. I think all
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Members would agree that whatever funds the federal Government provides for health care and post-secondary education, the federal authority, in order to carry out its responsibilities, must make sure that those funds are spent well and efficiently from an administrative point of view for the delivery of health and educational services by the provinces.
We say there is probably a greater need for the federal Government to examine more closely, through agreed upon audit procedures, how well the provinces are distributing those funds, whether or not they are being distributed for purposes that they were intended, and if they are not, whether funds are withheld. That is perfectly legitimate. So a province such as British Columbia, as my colleague who spoke earlier mentioned, cannot, so to speak, abscond with funds meant for universities and then put them into something else. In other words, their funds are conditional on their being spent for what they were meant to be spent on, and that they are administered efficiently.
When you consider the economic conditions of Canada's population over the last few years and the way they are likely to be for the next two or three years, this is the worst time of all to reduce the amount that we should be contributing in both health care and post-secondary education. Today, we are experiencing a depression. In previous depressions we were always asked where we would get the money. Tommy Douglas quoted a Minister of Finance at that time who asked a young person whether he thought money grows on gooseberry bushes. When the war started in September, 1939, Tommy said that they found the bush. There was lots of money at that time.
In times of economic depression, when Governments are having difficulty in obtaining funds, that is the worst and least valid kind of argument to make. Governments can arrange financing much easier than individuals, universities or hospitals.
The most positive aspect of it is that the nation as a whole shares in the cost, whether it is through current tax revenues or borrowed funds which are repaid by future tax revenues.
Today, tens of thousands of people are lining up at food banks-a euphemistic name for soup kitchens-in scores of cities throughout the country. Furthermore, a higher proportion of our population is elderly and in need of health care. Therefore, this is the worst time for the Government to be reneging on a fifty-fifty agreement. This is the worst time and these are the worst areas in which to hold down or reduce expenditures in the name of deficit reduction. In fact, any self-respecting Government would not even consider these as programs to hold down or reduce expenditures. In light of today's conditions, the Government should be expanding those facilities.
Even during the "hungry thirties", a Conservative and Liberal Government brought in better care for tubercular and cancer patients when there was little or no money available

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
because that was the best time to bring in those kinds of programs.
The federal Government should tell the provinces that it will continue its 50/50 sharing, including sharing the cost if the provinces wish to improve or expand their health care systems or university programs, as long as they are in accordance with the agreement and respect the conditions under which the money is provided.
Provinces should be able to provide financial and equipment incentives to the medical profession so that there is a better distribution of doctors in our smaller cities and remote areas. Their respective medical care plans should provide extra money, housing and medical equipment to those doctors as an incentive to go to the remote and the small cities in order that there will be a more equitable distribution of doctors in this country.
I recently saw a television program describing the latest equipment that technology has developed. This equipment, whether it is a kidney dialysis machine or heart transplant equipment, costs hundreds of thousands of dollars. There must be a fifty-fifty cost sharing for the provision of that equipment not only in big city hospitals but throughout the country.
Let me deal with ambulance services. I have a close friend who worked in the ambulance industry. He told me that it is safer and quicker to take a taxi to the hospital if one is suffering from a heart attack. He described a situation where the most experienced paramedic would drive the ambulance while the new recruit would look after the patient in the back. Ambulance services should not be subject to the profit considerations of a private owner. They should be owned and operated by hospitals, the municipalities or the provincial Department of Health. Those services should be completely under the authority of the health care department of the province or municipality. We should spend millions of dollars on paramedic training. There is a distinct shortage of paramedics in this country, for which there is no excuse.
Also, as Canadian nurses have informed us, many hospitals are understaffed. There is no reason why any federal or provincial Government cannot provide adequate nursing and a proper distribution of those nurses. That cost must be shared 50/50. Let us consider home care. Millions of dollars could be saved if people were looked after in their homes rather than occupying hospital beds. There is a great need for chronic care beds for people who are not ill enough to remain in a hospital bed but are too ill to be at home. There are waiting lists as long as your arm for chronic care beds in every city of this country. The federal Government should be willing to share the cost if the provinces and territories increase the number of chronic care beds.
Midwifery is another area in which child birth, under the supervision of the medical and nursing profession, can take place in the home or hospital without the necessity of a physician being in full-time attendance. This may be opposed
by some in the College of Physicians and Surgeons, but that is too bad.
Holland provides marvellous home care, chronic care and midwifery systems in conjunction with its medical practitioners. Countries such as Holland have led the way in these areas.
This is no time for the Government to be chiselling the amount of money it contributes. I do not know of any taxpayers who object to their tax money being spent for these purposes. I believe they would even accept an increase, as long as those taxes were fairly applied. I do not believe any Canadian wants to see those services restricted or cut back. Instead, they want a well managed and efficiently run health care system with well trained practitioners and enough equipment so that there will be equal opportunity for treatment for all Canadians, no matter where they live.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that Conservative Members are not standing up to defend Bill C-96. Is it any wonder that they are not defending an otherwise indefensible piece of regressive legislation?
This legislation illustrates the Government's problem with respect to integrity and credibility. During the last election campaign, the Conservative Party made well over 300 promises. One of the major promises it made was that it would not reduce federal transfer payments to the provinces but in fact would increase those payments. That was a promise made in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on July 26, 1984.
The Conservative caucus promised that they would respect the federal obligation to fund provincial health care through established programs financing and make additional funds available to the provinces on a cost shared basis for the Established Programs Financing Act and make additional funds available to the provinces on a cost shared basis for the establishment or enrichment of programs deemed most likely to improve the general level of health and limit long-term costs. That was the promise, and what has the Government decided to do with respect to that particular promise? It has decided not only to break that promise but to breach a previous commitment made by the Liberal administration to provide an adequate level of funding to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education. There was an agreement in place with the provinces. They fully expected to receive a specific amount of money from the federal Government in order to fund health care and post-secondary education. This Government has decided unilaterally to breach that particular agreement. It has decided to transfer to the provinces over the course of the next six years $8 billion less than what the provincial Governments expected to receive under the previous commitment.
What happened to the promise of consultation? What happened to the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) after the last national election campaign that the country had embarked upon a new era of national reconciliation? You will recall those words, Mr. Speaker. I ask, where is the new era of
May 6, 1986

national reconciliation? Because not one single, solitary provincial Government has agreed to the specific measures contained in Bill C-96. In fact, the provincial Governments have roundly condemned the federal Government for breaching the previous commitment and threatening the very foundation of Confederation by withdrawing over $8 billion, which would otherwise have been transferred to the provinces over the next six years.
David Peterson, the Premier of Ontario, pointed out to the Prime Minister at the First Ministers' Conference that what the Government was intending to do was to transfer the national problem, the national deficit, to the provincial Governments. Mr. Nixon, the Ontario Treasurer, pointed out that there was a uniform opposition to Ottawa's plan. Nobody thought it was a good idea. Mr. Gerard Levesque, the Quebec Finance Minister, said it was not fair to the provinces because they had been counting on the amounts agreed to in the accords.
Notwithstanding the universal opposition of the provincial Premiers and Ministers of Finance, the Government decided to cut $8 billion.
The Government has decided to cut just under $3 billion in provincial transfer payments over the next six years to the Province of Ontario. I note that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) is in the Chamber today. I would like to point out to him, if he is not already aware of it, that in his home Province of Newfoundland there will be a reduction of $188 million. Where was the Minister of Justice when that particular decision was made? Was he consulted? Did the Minister of Justice, the Minister responsible for Newfoundland, stand up in Cabinet for the people of his home province? Of course he did not. He was afraid. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister said: "Sorry, notwithstanding your protestations, we are still going to cut $188 million in federal transfer payments to the Province of Newfoundland over the next six years".
What impact will that cut have on the province of the Minister of Justice? The Conservative provincial Government of Newfoundland will be faced with some very difficult decisions. No doubt that provincial Government, along with other provincial Governments, will have to cut back in the area of health care and education. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we in Canada are blessed with the best health care system and post-secondary education in the world. As a result of the actions of the Government, that particular level of health care and post-secondary education is being threatened. It is unfair, regressive and, as I indicated earlier, it is a threat to the very basic roots of Confederation.
There are tough decisions which have to be made by the provincial Governments. The provincial Government of Ontario will be without $3 billion in federal transfer payments over the next six years. The Government knows that the only way the province could remedy that particular situation is either to raise taxes or to cut services. There is not much of a choice when the federal Government decides to withdraw $3 billion from the economy of the Province of Ontario. It is not
Federal- Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
fair that that particular Government has either to raise taxes or to reduce expenditures. If the province does decide to reduce expenditures, there will have to be cuts in health care and postsecondary education. The high level of health care we have learned to appreciate will be seriously affected. Provincial Governments will have to close hospitals, cut the number of hospital beds and cut back on such things as cancer research. The universities will have to cut back on the number of courses which are taught and cut back on staff. They will have to increase tuition fees. They might even have to consider charging other forms of user fees in order to make up the shortfall.
Why is the federal Government doing what it is doing? It is obvious that it is absolutely paranoid about the federal deficit. We on this side of the House are concerned about the deficit. We believe that Governments should be fiscally responsible and that we should not spend money without consideration of our national debt. However, if the goal is to reduce the deficit, surely it must be done on a fair basis. It must not be done on the backs of the disadvantaged. Surely it should not be done in a way that would threaten the quality of health care and postsecondary education.
Rather than recognize the serious implications of the measures it is about to take in Bill C-96, the Government is prepared, in order to reduce the deficit and to satisfy its friends on Bay Street and wealthy corporations, to have the average Canadian suffer and simply to push the deficit on to the laps of the provincial Governments. It is patently unfair. Certainly the provincial Governments and all other interest groups will take the opportunity to appear before the committee when this particular Bill is referred to committee. I hope that the Minister of Justice will appear to defend the federal Government on this particular piece of legislation. The people of Newfoundland will be out close to $200 million over the next six years as a result of the broken promise of this particular federal Government. I hope that the Minister will at least have the courage of his convictions and will stand up and explain that to the people of his province.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few remarks about Bill C-96, a most unfortunate Bill which will reduce the growth rate of the federal per capita transfers to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education. These transfers are an important federal contribution which help provinces meet their constitutional responsibility for the areas of health and post-secondary education, which make sure that people all across Canada have access to more or less the same standards of health care and post-secondary education, and which use the ability of the federal Government to raise revenue through taxes, an ability which is greater than that of the provinces, to make sure that the provinces are able to provide adequate services.

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Over the next five years, Bill C-96 will see some $5 billion cut from the ability of the provinces to spend on health and post-secondary education. This amount is cumulative. It begins with a relatively minor amount and then builds up each year until it will total $5 billion by 1991. It is slowly but surely undermining a system that has been built up by previous generations. The effects of Bill C-96 will not be felt too much at first but will be devastating in its final impact.
Perhaps I could use British Columbia as an example. In 1986-87, the current fiscal year, British Columbia stands to lose some $36.8 million as a result of this Bill. Next year that figure will be $77.4 million, the year after $123.7 million, then $173.8 million, and in 1990-91, the figure will be $230 million for a total of $641.8 million over the next five years.
If we had listened to and believed what Conservative Members said when they were in opposition or when they were campaigning during the last federal election, we would be in a state of shock because of the Bill before us. I am sure some Canadians must be in a state of shock, particularly those who were naive enough to have listened to what Conservative Members were saying without listening to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) said between the lines.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) had this to say regarding Bill C-12, the Liberal Government's six and five program:
First and foremost, Bill C-12 is still a tax grab by the Government. In the 1983-84 fiscal year the Government is able to reduce its projected transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education by almost $120 million and next year that reduction will amount to $260 million. That is the kind of tax grab the Government is getting into with this Bill.
The Minister, when she was in opposition, was concerned about a tax grab of $260 million under the 6-and 5-program. Now we are talking about a tax grab of some $5 billion, and she is applauding it.
During the 1984 election campaign, members of the Progressive Conservative Party stated the following:
We are committed to sustaining the current federal financial commitment, according to the formula set out in the 1977 Agreement... We believe that financing of post-secondary education is an important priority for both levels of governments.
That commitment was made during the election campaign. Where is that commitment today? Just like so many other commitments Conservative Members made, it is forgotten in their blind fixation on reducing the deficit.

speechtext:
What we need in writing is the resignations of some of those Ministers over there.
The effect of this Bill will be a two-tiered health care system. Dr. Bill Vail of the Canadian Medical Association, in response to the tabling of this Bill, said the following:
We will have one quality of health care in the rich provinces and second or third rate services in the poor provinces. The dream of Canadians of having access to reasonably comparable health services, no matter where they live or travel, appears to have been abandoned by the Government of Canada.
Dr. Vail went on to point out that the provinces that are going to be particularly affected by this are Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and, to some extent, Quebec and Manitoba. Where are the members of the Conservative Party from those provinces? Why are they not speaking up against this Bill which will have such a disastrous effect on health care in their provinces?
The Canadian Association of University Teachers pointed out that cuts to post-secondary education are going to mean a $1.7 billion shortfall over the next five years. What will be the results of this $1.7 billion shortfall? It will mean that there will be restricted enrolment. There will be increased fees, and that will mean that the children of rich parents will be able to get into universities from which the children of middle-income, working-class parents will be excluded. Children from communities that are far away from university centres will not have access to education because they will not be able to pay the additional tuition costs as well as the higher costs for room and board.
The $1.7 billion shortfall will result in lower standards of teaching and in less research taking place in colleges and universities. In short, the shortfall will result in second-rate universities and second-rate graduates. The result of second-rate graduates will be a second-rate country as a result of this second-rate Government's legislation. Where is the pursuit of excellence about which Conservative Members spoke when they were running for office?
Time after time, we on this side of the House have spoken of the Tory fixation on the deficit. We agree that the deficit is something that has to be looked at with concern, but how are Tory Members dealing with it? They are dealing with it by cutting back in ways that will harm our country's future. Our Party has made a number of suggestions as to how the deficit should be approached, including a system of fair taxes in which everyone pays their fair share, the elimination of waste and the creation of jobs. We should put people back to work instead of cutting back on essential services like health care and post-secondary education.
Those of us who come from British Columbia saw the results of this kind of idiotic cut-back mentality in the last four years. Cut-backs have created a deliberate depression in British Columbia. I would like to remind Hon. Members from all sides of the House that British Columbia is the only province in Canada in which the employment rate has not yet recovered to pre-recession levels. There are 50,000 fewer people working in British Columbia today than in 1981. That is a direct result of the kind of cut-backs that the Province of British Columbia has been implementing over the last four years, the kind of

cut-backs that we are seeing implemented by the present Conservative Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are currently debating a motion that this House declines to proceed with a Bill, the princple of which is to reduce unilaterally payments by the federal Government to the provinces for vital health care and post-secondary education services.
There are a number of things which are very much wrong with this Bill. I do not think we can stress too often one of the most serious failures of the Bill, that is, through this Bill the Government is proceeding unilaterally to cut some $8 billion out of moneys which would otherwise go to the provinces for worth-while programs such as health care and post-secondary education. The Government may argue that this measure was already announced, or at least foreshadowed in its May, 1985 Budget, but that is not really the case. The Budget Speech did refer to a reduction of the federal EPF contributions, but made no mention of the date on which it would take effect. If one refers to Table 2.1 of the fiscal plan and Table 2, Chapter 5, of

May 6, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
the Budget Papers published in May, 1985, one would find there no indication of a reduction for the fiscal year 1986-87. This shows that the Government was probably planning at that time to introduce changes at the end of the normal five-year term, that is, on April 1, 1987.
The Government waited until the Annual First Ministers' Conference, which was held on November 28 and 29, 1985, in Halifax, to make the formal announcement of specific changes and of the date on which they would take effect.
Why did the Government change its mind between the May 1985 Budget and the November 1985 Halifax Conference and decide to move the date ahead? To understand that move by the Government, we have to recall that this period coincides with the Government's decision to reimburse the uninsured depositors of the two failed banks, as a result of which the Government, I suggest, realized that it would not be able to achieve the deficit reduction objective it had set for itself. After bungling the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, the Government had to find the money somewhere to make up for its poor handling of that banking situation. It can therefore be argued that the depositors of the bankrupt banks were reimbursed, at least in part, by funds which would otherwise have been used to enhance the quality of our educational system and our health care services.
Finally, it should be noted that the February 1986 Budget pretty well ignored this new measure despite the fact that it is to take effect, if the House makes the mistake of approving it, on April 1, 1986.
Let me again stress, as has already been stressed in this debate, that the only reason offered by the Government to justify this cut-back is the effort which all Canadians and all provinces must make, so the Government claims, to reduce the federal deficit. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has acknowledged that he is transferring part of his deficit to the provinces, but he has argued that this transfer is a problem of lesser importance than that of the deficit. In other words, this heartless Government is cutting health care for seniors and for middle and lower-income Canadians and making it impossible for tens of thousands of middle and low-income young people to go to university. That does not matter so long as the Government can reduce the deficit. How cruel, how misguided and how wrong! Certainly, if one is concerned about the deficit, economic growth and the greater revenues which come from that, and having a more efficient, productive and healthy population, that is a better way of tackling the deficit, if it must be tackled at all, than by cutting $8 billion from moneys the federal Government had promised to the provinces. That was money which was going to be spent, and which would have been spent, to improve post-secondary education and health care, if not just to maintain existing standards for millions and millions of Canadians in every province.
The record is clear. Beginning with this Bill, the Government has acted unilaterally, without consent of the provinces,
and has failed to respect the tradition of federal-provincial agreements. The EPF Program is administered under a federal Act and we have to admit that technically speaking, it can be changed by the federal Parliament unilaterally without the formal consent of the provinces. However, the tradition has been to renegotiate, and I stress the word "renegotiate", these fiscal arrangements every five years.
This Act was amended for the first time in 1982 and the provincial Governments expected to be able to renegotiate shortly the new arrangements that would take effect as of April 1, 1987. The Conservative Government has thus failed to respect the long-standing tradition and has unilaterally announced amendments that would take effect a year ahead of the normal date of expiry of the agreement. No wonder that, when the federal Government announced its intentions at the federal-provincial conference, the representatives of the provinces unanimously rejected the federal proposal.
The premiers rejected the proposal, whether they were members of the Conservative Party or of other Parties. They rose to say that what the federal Government was doing was wrong. It was adding to the burden of the provinces the effort of the federal Government to cut the deficit. It was adding to the burden of the provinces the desires of the federal Government ahead of the responsibilities of the provinces to their populations; in effect, the same populations about which the federal Government should be concerned when it comes to maintaining and improving standards of health care and postsecondary education.
Once again, let us look at what the provinces will have to do as a result of the cuts in transfers of funds required by the provinces, cuts totalling $8 billion by 1991-92. What are the alternatives the provinces have? As a result of these cuts, the provinces will be forced to increase taxes as one alternative. Another alternative is to increase deficits and another would be to rethink priorities and cut back on services accordingly.
The Conservative Government might well be forcing provinces to reduce the number of hospital beds. The Conservative Government, through this legislation, might well be forcing the provinces to restrict the number of students who are admitted to universities and colleges across the country. The Conservative Government, through this legislation, might well be forcing the provinces to increase fees paid by consumers of provincial services. This might cause provinces to increase or institute hospital user fees and might force provinces to increase or institute tuition fees at universities and other post-secondary education institutions. Whatever method is adopted by the provinces, it is the individual taxpayer who will bear the cost of the cut-backs, and that without any benefit whatsoever accruing to the individual Canadian and his or her family.
It is very clear why we moved this motion. When we look at the evidence, we find that the Conservative Government broke its promise to consult with the provinces before doing anything like this. Minister of Justice rose to speak just now, he happened to be the very first Government Member and the first Minister to speak to this subject before the House.
The Bill was introduced in the House by the Parliamentary Secretary. I was there. I remember clearly it was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott). There wasn't a single Minister who had the guts to rise in the House and introduce a Bill as sordid as this one. And now, after several days of debate, we see the Minister of Justice rise in the House and take ten minutes or so to make an outrageous speech, livened up with jokes that would be more appropriate in a zoo than in the serious debate we are having today.
The Minister started by explaining why the Bill was proposed in the House in the first place. According to him, it was to make up for the mistakes of the previous Government which had accumulated deficit after deficit. Well, my opinion is slightly different, and I would say that the Government has added to the deficit by introducing measures to suit its friends.
Mr. Speaker, the Government's decision to give people in a position to make capital gains in this country a lifetime exemption of up to $500,000 will cost Canadian taxpayers, both rich and poor, something like $4.5 billion between now and 1990. And I don't want to hear the excuse that payments to the provinces are only being cut back in an attempt to reduce a deficit that was accumulated by the previous Government, because I would say to the Government: Today, you give handouts to your friends, and you ask the little man, the average taxpayer and low-income Canadians to foot the bill.
Let us talk about the rescue operations for the two banks that went belly up in western Canada. When the Government came to the House begging for billions, it was to bail out people with deposits in excess of $60,000, not ordinary people who were already covered under deposit insurance.
